brief: Given n cities with coordinates, each city gets power either by building a station (cost c_i) or by wiring to a powered city; a wire between i and j costs (k_i + k_j) times Manhattan distance. Find the minimum total cost plus the stations and wires.
key_idea: Add a virtual node 0 with edge 0-i of weight c_i; the answer is the MST over this graph, and the dense edge weights mean Prim in O(n^2).
solution: 1. Treat city 0 as a virtual source: edge (0, i) has weight c_i (building a station at i).
2. Edge (i, j) has weight (k_i + k_j) * (|x_i - x_j| + |y_i - y_j|).
3. Run Prim from node 0 on the complete graph of n+1 nodes, O(n^2), keeping for each node the best incoming edge (parent).
4. Each node added with parent 0 is a power station; every other node adds the wire (parent, node).
5. Sum of the chosen edge weights is the minimum cost. Use long long: the largest edge is about 2e9 * 2e6 = 4e15.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Pick city 1 (d=3, station), then city 3 (d=3, station): total=8, all stations, matches the expected 8.

brief: Bacteria start as one bacterium of mass 1. Each day any bacteria may split into two halves; each night every bacterium gains 1 mass. Given n, find the minimum number of nights to reach total mass exactly n and the number of splits on each day (or -1).
key_idea: Let c_i be the bacteria count after day i's splits; total mass is 1 + sum of c_i, with c_0=1, c_{i-1} <= c_i <= 2c_{i-1}, so the task is a sum of c_1..c_d = n-1 with minimal d; -1 never occurs.
solution: 1. Let T = n-1. The largest sum with d nights is 2+4+...+2^d = 2^(d+1)-2, so d is the smallest d with 2^(d+1)-2 >= T.
2. Keep p = current count (starts at 1) and R = remaining sum to place (starts at T).
3. For step i with rem = d-i+1 steps left, pick x = min(2p, R/rem): the largest legal count that still leaves room for the rest.
4. Splits on day i = x - p; then R -= x and p = x.
5. Greedy always ends with R = 0, so the answer always exists (the -1 case never happens). Verified by brute force for n = 2..3000 in this run.
complexity: O(log n) per test case, O(log n) space
dry_run: Sample n=9: T=8, smallest d with 2^(d+1)-2 >= 8 is d=3.
Day 3: rem=1, x=min(6, 3)=3, split 0, R=0. Output 3 nights, splits 1 1 0 (valid; sample shows 1 0 2 and any answer is accepted).
Check: mass = 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9.

brief: An n x n board has a value in each cell. Place two bishops so that no cell is attacked by both; a cell attacked by exactly one bishop adds its value. Maximize the total and output one optimal placement.
key_idea: Diagonal sums are precomputed; a bishop at (i,j) attacks sum(i+j diagonal) + sum(i-j diagonal) - a[i][j]. Bishops on opposite colours never share a cell, so take the best cell of each parity.
solution: 1. Read the grid and accumulate s1[i+j] (anti-diagonal sum) and s2[i-j+n] (diagonal sum).
2. For every cell compute v = s1[i+j] + s2[i-j+n] - a[i][j], the total attacked by a bishop there.
3. Split cells by colour parity (i+j) mod 2 and keep the maximum v and its cell for each parity.
4. Answer = best of parity 0 + best of parity 1; print the two cells as the placement.
5. Edge case: n >= 2 guarantees both colours exist, and values are >= 0 so long long sums are safe.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(n) extra space beyond the grid
dry_run: Sample: the program prints 12 and bishops (2,2) [even] and (3,2) [odd], matching the expected output.
Own example: grid [[1,2],[3,4]]. Anti-diagonal sums s1: idx2=1, idx3=5, idx4=4. Diagonal sums s2 (i-j+n): idx1=2, idx2=5, idx3=3.
Total 5+5=10, which is correct: bishop (1,1) hits cells 1 and 4, bishop (1,2) hits cells 2 and 3, no overlap.

brief: The year has n months with d_i days each and the calendar wraps around. Visiting on day j gives j hugs. Pick x consecutive days (possibly crossing into the next year) and maximize the total hugs.
key_idea: The best window can always end on the last day of some month, so for each end month find the window start with a binary search on prefix day counts and add the partial-month arithmetic sum.
solution: 1. Double the month array (2n months) and build prefix sums of days PD and of hugs PH, where a full month of length d gives d(d+1)/2 hugs.
2. For each end month i in [n, 2n), the window ends at day d_i of month i.
3. Binary search the largest j in [i-n+1, i] with days(j..i) >= x; this is the month where the window starts.
4. Full months j+1..i contribute PH[i+1]-PH[j+1]; the remaining r = x - days(j+1..i) days are the last r days of month j, contributing r*(2d_j - r + 1)/2.
5. Answer = max over all end months. Edge cases: x = total days (full year) and r = d_j (whole month) both work; use long long since sums reach about 1e17.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 3: n=5, x=6, d=[4,2,3,1,3]. Consider the window that ends on day 4 of the month with d=4.
Full months after the start month: that window needs 6 days, so the last 4 days (4,3,2,1 of the d=4 month) give 10 hugs; r=2 days remain.
The start month is the previous month (d=3): its last r=2 days are 3 and 2, giving 5 hugs.
Total 10+5=15, which matches the expected answer 15.

brief: Build an n x m matrix of 0s and 1s in which every row has exactly a ones and every column has exactly b ones, or report NO if it is impossible. Multiple test cases.
key_idea: Counting the ones gives the only necessary condition n*a = m*b; when it holds, fill row i with the cells (i*a + k) mod m for k = 0..a-1 in a cyclic sweep.
solution: 1. If n*a != m*b, print NO (the total number of ones is counted two ways).
2. Otherwise print YES and build each row as a string of m zeros.
3. For row i, set positions (i*a + k) mod m to '1' for k = 0..a-1; since a <= m the positions in a row are distinct.
4. Over all rows the ones fill a continuous cyclic sweep of n*a = m*b cells, so each column is hit exactly b times.
5. Edge case: the statement gives 1 <= a <= m and 1 <= b <= n, so no out-of-range issues.
complexity: O(n*m) time per test case for output, O(m) extra space per row
dry_run: Sample n=3, m=6, a=2, b=1: n*a = 6 = m*b, so YES.
Row 0 takes positions 0,1 -> 110000; row 1 takes 2,3 -> 001100; row 2 takes 4,5 -> 000011.
Every column has exactly one '1' (b=1) and every row has two (a=2), matching the sample's validity requirement.
Sample 2: n=2, m=2, a=2, b=1: n*a=4 != 2 = m*b, so the answer is NO.

brief: Vertices 1..n are joined when their XOR is prime. Colour all vertices with the fewest colours so that adjacent vertices differ, and print the count and a colouring. Up to 500 test cases, sum of n up to 2e5.
key_idea: Vertices with the same value mod 4 have XOR divisible by 4 (never prime), so 4 colours always work; the minimum is 1,2,3 for n=1, n<=3, n=4..5, and 4 for n>=6 (K4 on {1,3,4,6}).
solution: 1. Two vertices equal mod 4 have XOR divisible by 4, which is never prime, so colour v with (v mod 4)+1 for n >= 6 and use 4 colours.
2. For n in 2..5 the pairs {2k, 2k+1} differ by XOR 1 (not prime), so colour v with (v>>1)+1 instead, giving 2 colours for n<=3 and 3 colours for n=4..5.
3. Minimality: n=2,3 has an edge, so 2 colours are needed; {1,3,4} is a triangle for n>=4 (XOR 2,5,7 all prime), and {1,3,4,6} is K4 for n>=6.
4. Print k, then the n colours on one line.
5. Edge case: n=1 has a single vertex and one colour.
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(1) extra space besides the output
dry_run: Sample n=6 (>=6, mod-4 scheme): colour = (v mod 4)+1 for v=1..6 gives 2 3 4 1 2 3.
Check edge 1-6: XOR = 7 is prime, colours 2 and 3 differ.
Check edge 1-4: XOR = 5 is prime, colours 2 and 1 differ.
Output: k=4 and the colours 2 3 4 1 2 3 (valid; sample shows another valid colouring).

brief: n vertices with values a_i and no edges. Joining x and y costs a_x + a_y, and m special offers each join a pair for a given w. Find the minimum total cost to make the graph connected.
key_idea: Any ordinary edge (x,y) can be replaced by two edges through the cheapest vertex m, since a_m + a_x <= a_x + a_y; so the candidate edges are the n-1 star edges from m plus the offers, and Kruskal gives the answer.
solution: 1. Find the vertex mn with the smallest a. Build candidate edges (a_mn + a_i, mn, i) for every i != mn.
2. Add every offer (w, x, y) as a candidate edge.
3. Sort all candidate edges by cost (ties do not matter).
4. Run Kruskal with DSU: take an edge if its endpoints are in different components and add its cost.
5. Output the total. Edge case: n = 1 has no edges and the answer is 0; sums reach about 4e17, so use long long.
complexity: O((n+m) log(n+m)) time, O(n+m) space
dry_run: Sample 2: a=[1,3,3,7], min vertex 1. Star edges: (1,2)=4, (1,3)=4, (1,4)=8; no offers; sorted and all taken: 4+4+8=16.
Take (2,1,1): total 1. Star (1,2) skipped (same set). Take star (1,3)=4: total 5. Offer (2,3,5) skipped.
Output 5, which matches the expected output.

brief: Given a connected weighted graph, choose a spanning tree whose edge weights have the smallest possible bitwise OR, and print that OR. Multiple test cases separated by blank lines.
key_idea: Decide the answer bit by bit from the top: try to clear each bit, and keep it cleared only if the edges whose weight is a submask of the candidate still connect the graph.
solution: 1. Start with ans = 2^30 - 1, which covers every weight (w <= 1e9 < 2^30) and is feasible since the graph is connected.
2. For bit b from 29 down to 0, set cand = ans with bit b cleared.
3. Run DSU using only the edges with (w & ~cand) == 0, i.e. weights that are submasks of cand.
4. If those edges connect all n vertices, set ans = cand; otherwise keep bit b.
5. Print ans after all bits. Each test resets the DSU for its n vertices; total work is about 30*(n+m) per test.
complexity: O(30 * (n + m) * alpha(n)) time, O(n + m) space
dry_run: Clearing high bits keeps all edges, so ans shrinks to 3 (bits 0 and 1 remain).
Clear bit 1: cand=1, only w=1 edge usable, graph not connected, so bit 1 stays: ans=3.
Clear bit 0: cand=2, edges 2-3 and 1-3 (w=2) connect everything, so ans=2. Output 2, matching the expected output.

brief: A bag of size n must be filled exactly with boxes whose sizes are powers of two; a box can be split into two equal halves. Find the minimum number of splits needed, or -1 if impossible. Multiple test cases.
key_idea: Process the bits of n from low to high, borrowing the smallest larger box when a needed bit has no box, and merging unused equal boxes upward; the total splits is the sum of distances borrowed.
solution: 1. Count boxes by exponent cnt[k] (box size 2^k) and compute the total sum; if sum < n print -1.
2. For bit k from low to high: if n has bit k set and cnt[k] = 0, find the smallest j > k with cnt[j] > 0.
3. Split one 2^j box down to 2^k: this costs j-k divisions and leaves one spare piece of each size 2^k..2^(j-1); add them to cnt.
4. Use one 2^k piece for this bit (cnt[k] -= 1), then merge leftover pairs upward: cnt[k+1] += cnt[k] / 2.
5. Sum of costs is the answer. Use long long: n is up to 1e18.
complexity: O(m + 60*60) time per test (the borrow loop is at most 60 steps per bit), O(60) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=10 (binary 1010), boxes 1,32,1 so cnt[0]=2, cnt[5]=1.
Bit 0 (0 in n): merge the two 1s into one 2: cnt[1]=1.
Bit 1 (set): cnt[1]=1, use it: cnt[1]=0.
Bit 3 (set): cnt[3]=0, borrow 32 (j=5): cost 2, leftovers cnt[3]=1, cnt[4]=1; use the 8, cnt[3]=0.
Answer 2, which matches the expected output.

brief: Given an array a of n values, perform operations x = 1..n-1 in order; operation x adds an edge (u,v) with u != v and x dividing |a_u - a_v|. Make the graph connected with these n-1 edges or report No; print Yes with the edges otherwise. Multiple test cases.
key_idea: Each operation must join two different components, and the tree needs one edge per modulus; the statement was fetched, but I did not find a provably correct construction, so no code is given.
solution: 1. Model it as a rainbow spanning tree: pick n-1 tree edges and assign each one a distinct operation x that divides its value difference.
2. Operation 1 accepts any pair, so colour 1 is free; for x >= 2 an edge is usable only if x divides the difference.
3. Greedy (take any cross-component pair valid for x) gets stuck often: on random arrays with n <= 9 about 30% of runs fail, so the choice of edge matters.
4. Exhaustive search over all choices found no unsolvable array for n <= 5 (random values up to 30), which suggests the answer is Yes often, but this is not proven.
5. A correct but heavy route is matroid intersection of the graphic matroid with a transversal matroid on the operation labels; I did not implement it.
complexity: not determined; the matroid-intersection route is roughly O(n^2 * n) with large constants
dry_run: Own example: n=2, a=[1,4]. Operation 1 (x=1) accepts any pair, so join 2 and 1: the graph is connected and the answer is Yes with edge 2 1.

Own example: n=3, a=[1,2,4]. Op 1 joins 1 and 2 (any pair). Op 2 needs a cross-component pair with even difference: 3 (value 4) and 1 (value 1) differ by 3, not valid; 3 and 2 differ by 2, valid, so join 3 2.
Both examples are checked by hand; the general case is not solved here.

brief: An array a of n positive integers can be changed by moving one unit from a_i to a_{i+1} (decrease a_i, increase a_{i+1}) any number of times. Find the minimum possible value of max(a) - min(a). Many test cases.
key_idea: Units only move right, so a final array b is reachable iff its total is S and every prefix sum B_i <= A_i; for a window [L, L+d] this reduces to O(n) checks, with L chosen as large as possible, and binary search on d.
solution: 1. Let A be the prefix sums and S = A_n. Final prefix sums must satisfy B_i <= A_i with B_n = S.
2. For a final range [L, R], the prefix condition forces i*L <= A_i, so take L = min(S/n, min over i<n of floor(A_i / i)).
3. With R = L + d, the array is feasible iff n*R >= S and A_j + (n-j)*R >= S for all j in 1..n-1.
4. Feasibility is monotone in d, so binary search the smallest d in [0, 2e12] that passes the check.
5. Edge cases: n = 1 gives 0 (the checks reduce to R >= L); sums and products reach about 2e17, so use long long.
complexity: O(n log C) time per test case, C = 2e12, O(n) space
dry_run: Answer 1, which matches the expected output.

brief: A connected graph of n fields with m roads, k special fields. Bessie walks a shortest path from field 1 to n. Add exactly one new road between two different special fields to maximize the resulting shortest distance, and print that distance.
key_idea: BFS from 1 (d1) and from n (dn); a new road u-v gives distance min(D, d1[u]+1+dn[v], d1[v]+1+dn[u]); sort specials by d1 and use a suffix maximum of dn.
solution: 1. BFS from field 1 to get d1, and from field n to get dn; let D = d1[n].
2. Sort the special fields by d1 ascending.
3. Build suffix maxima suf[i] = max dn over specials with index >= i in that order.
4. For each i, the road from special i to the best later special gives min(D, d1[s_i] + 1 + suf[i+1]); take the maximum over i.
5. Print the maximum. Verified against exhaustive pairs on 400 random small graphs.
complexity: O(n + m) time for two BFS plus O(k log k) sorting, O(n + m) space
dry_run: Sample 2: path 1-2-3-4-5, specials 2 and 4, D = 4.
Specials sorted by d1: field 2 (d1=1, dn=3), then field 4 (d1=3, dn=1).
i=0: min(4, d1[2]+1+dn[4]) = min(4, 1+1+1) = 3. Output 3, matching the expected answer.

brief: Given a lowercase string s of length n, find the minimum number of adjacent swaps needed to turn it into its reverse.
key_idea: Match the k-th copy of each letter in s to the k-th copy of that letter in reverse(s); the swap count is the number of inversions of that permutation, counted with a Fenwick tree.
solution: 1. Let t = reverse(s). For each letter, record its positions in t in increasing order.
2. Scan s left to right; the k-th occurrence of letter c in s gets target index = k-th occurrence of c in t, giving a permutation perm.
3. Equal letters keep their relative order, so each swap fixes exactly one inversion of perm: the answer is the inversion count of perm.
4. Count inversions with a Fenwick tree: for each i, add (i - number of earlier values <= perm[i]).
5. Edge case: a palindrome gives perm = identity and answer 0; n up to 2e5 needs a long long answer (up to about 2e10).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: s=aaaza, t=azaaa. perm from s-order: [0,2,3,1,4] (the z at s[3] maps to t[1]).
Inversions in perm: (2,1) at indices 1,3 and (3,1) at indices 2,3, so 2 pairs.
Output 2, matching the expected output.
Sample 2: cbaabc is a palindrome, so perm is the identity and the answer is 0.

brief: Given arrays a and b (b_i in {0,1}) and k, spend at most k increments, each on an index with b_i = 1. The score is max over i of a_i + median(a without element i). Output the maximum score. Many test cases.
key_idea: The median of the other n-1 elements is >= T iff at least h = ceil(n/2) of them are >= T; for a b=1 index all leftover ops go to it, and for a b=0 index binary search T with a cost computed from prefix sums of the b=1 values.
solution: 1. Let h = ceil(n/2). Median of the others is >= T iff at least h others are >= T.
2. If b_i = 1: spend all k on a_i and take the target T as the h-th largest of the other values; candidate = a_i + k + that value.
3. If b_i = 0: find the largest T with cost <= k, where cost = 0 if at least h others are >= T, else the cheapest r = h - (count >= T) b=1 values below T are raised to T (sum of T - v).
4. Binary search T for each b_i = 0 index; the count and prefix sums come from sorted arrays, so each check is O(log n).
5. Answer = max over all candidates. Verified on the 8 sample cases and 300 random small cases against brute force over all op distributions.
complexity: O(n log n + n * log(maxA + k) * log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Index 3 (a=5, b=0): others are 2 (b=0), 1 (b=1), 1 (b=1). T=3: no others >= 3, so raise the two b=1 ones from 1 to 3, cost 2+2=4 <= 4: feasible.
T=4 would cost 3+3=6 > 4, so T0=3 and the candidate is 5+3=8.
Index 4 (a=1, b=1): others 2,1,5; h-th largest = 2; candidate 1+4+2=7. Max over all is 8, which matches the expected output.

brief: Split an array a of n integers into exactly k non-empty consecutive parts numbered 1..k from left to right. Each element's cost is its value times its part number. Maximize the total cost.
key_idea: Total cost = (sum of all a) + sum of suffix sums at the k-1 cut starts, so choose the k-1 largest suffix sums among positions 2..n.
solution: 1. Let suf[p] = a_p + ... + a_n, and S = suf[1].
2. Each element a_i gets 1 + (number of cuts at or before i). Summing gives S + sum over cut starts p of suf[p].
3. Cut starts are any k-1 distinct positions from 2..n, so take the k-1 largest suf[p] values.
4. Sort the suffix sums for p = 2..n in descending order and add the first k-1 to S.
5. Edge cases: k = 1 gives S alone; values reach about 3e11, so use long long.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Suffix sums for p=2..5: 7, 9, 4, 8. Largest one (k-1=1) is 9.
Answer 6 + 9 = 15, which matches the expected output.
Sample 3: n=4, k=1: no cuts, answer S = 3-1+6+0 = 8.

brief: Arrays a and b of length n can be reordered; removing one element from each array per operation until both have size k, minimize operations so that a_i < b_i for all paired i. For i = 1..m, replace a_1 by i and sum the minimum operation counts over all m arrays.
key_idea: The minimum operations equal max(0, max_v (#{a >= v} - #{b > v})) by Hall's theorem; a_1 = i adds 1 to the count for v <= i, so each i-term is a max of two prefix/suffix maxima over a step function.
solution: 1. Answer for one array = n - (max matching of pairs a < b) = max(0, max over v of (#{a >= v} - #{b > v})), by Hall's theorem on the a-side.
2. Let g(v) = #{a_2..a_n >= v} - #{b > v}; with a_1 = i, the value is max(0, max_{v<=i} g(v)+1, max_{v>i} g(v)).
3. g only changes at v = a_t + 1 and v = b_t, so store its constant pieces sorted by start, with prefix maxima and suffix maxima.
4. Walk the breakpoints in i over [1, m+1]: on each segment the value is constant, so add value * segment length (binary searches find the pieces).
5. Sum fits in long long; verified on the 4 samples and 300 random small cases by exhaustive matching.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test case, O(n) space
dry_run: i=3: c=[3,1]. Hall term at v=3: #{c>=3}=1, #{b>3}=0, so the value is 1 (one unmatched a).
Check by matching: 1<2 pairs, 3<3 fails, so the maximum matching is 1 and ops = 2-1 = 1.
Likewise i=1 and i=2 give 0 and i=4 gives 1, so the total is 0+0+1+1 = 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Given arrays a and b of length n, the beauty of b is the sum of |a_i - b_i|. With at most one operation (swap b_i and b_j for i < j), maximize the beauty and print it.
key_idea: Write |a_i-b_j| + |a_j-b_i| as the max over 4 sign patterns; then the gain of a swap is U_i + V_j for a fixed pattern, which is separable, so the best pair is found from the top two values of U and V.
solution: 1. base = sum |a_i - b_i|. Let g_i = |a_i - b_i|.
2. For each sign pair (s1, s2) in {+1,-1}^2 define U_i = s1*a_i - s2*b_i - g_i and V_i = s2*a_i - s1*b_i - g_i.
3. The swap gain for an unordered pair (i,j) is max over signs of U_i + V_j (since |x| = max(x, -x) for each term).
4. For each sign pattern take the best i != j of U_i + V_j using the top two values of U and of V (handling the case where both tops are the same index).
5. Answer = base + max(0, best gain over all patterns). Verified on the 6 samples and 400 random small cases against all swaps.
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(n) space
dry_run: Swap b_1 and b_2 gives b=[5,2]: |1-5| + |6-2| = 8, so gain = 6.
Best i != j: U_2 + V_1 = 10 + (-4) = 6, the gain; answer = 2 + 6 = 8, matching the direct swap.

brief: Three bags each hold a non-empty multiset. An operation takes a from one bag and b from another, removes b, and replaces a by a-b. Repeat until one number remains and output the largest possible final value.
key_idea: Each final sign pattern is a bipartite spanning tree between the '+' and '-' elements with edges only between different bags; the total negated set is either a whole bag or the minima of two different bags, so answer = total - 2 * min(those candidates).
solution: 1. Read the three bags, compute each bag sum S_k, minimum m_k and the grand total T.
2. The elements that end up with a minus sign form a set M; a valid M is either a whole bag (cost S_k) or the minimum of one bag plus the minimum of a different bag (cost m_i + m_j).
3. Minimise the negated cost C = min(S_1, S_2, S_3, m_1+m_2, m_1+m_3, m_2+m_3).
4. Answer = T - 2*C. Use long long: the total can reach 3e5 * 1e9.
5. Checked on both samples and 221 random tiny inputs against exhaustive search of the operations.
complexity: O(n1 + n2 + n3) time, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Candidates: S_1=3, S_3=5, S_2=18, m1+m2=4, m1+m3=6, m2+m3=8; the minimum is 3.
Answer 26 - 2*3 = 20, which matches the expected output.

brief: Given n and k (1 or 2), find the smallest x >= n whose decimal representation has no leading zero and uses at most k distinct digits. Up to 1e4 test cases with n up to 1e9.
key_idea: Try every allowed digit set D of size <= k; for each, find the smallest number >= n using only digits of D by keeping the longest matching prefix and bumping one digit, else go to length+1; take the minimum.
solution: 1. For k = 1 use sets {a}; for k = 2 use sets {a, b} with a <= b (both loops over 0..9, so 55 sets in total).
2. For a set D, let s be n as a string of length L. If every digit of s is in D, s is the answer.

3. Otherwise scan p from the longest valid prefix down to 0: keep s[0..p-1], replace s[p] by the smallest digit of D greater than s[p], and fill the rest with min(D). The first p that works gives the smallest same-length answer.
4. If no same-length answer exists, use length L+1 with the smallest nonzero digit of D first and min(D) for the rest.
5. Output the minimum over all sets. Checked on the 4 samples and 600 random tests against a linear search.
complexity: O(55 * 10) per test case (about 10 digit operations per set), O(1) space
dry_run: Sample n=177890, k=2, take D={1,8}: s = 1 7 7 8 9 0; the prefix '1' is in D, but s[1]=7 is not.
At p=1 bump: smallest digit in D greater than 7 is 8, so the prefix is '1' + '8' and the rest is min(D)=1 repeated 4 times.
Result 181111, which matches the expected output; other sets give larger candidates.
Sample n=998244353, k=1, D={9}: s starts 9,9 (both in D) then 8 is not, so pre=2. Bump at p=2: 9 > 8, giving prefix '999' then 9s for the rest: 999999999, which matches the expected output.

brief: n employees (n odd) each get an integer salary in [l_i, r_i], total at most s. Maximize the median salary and output it. Many test cases with sums of n up to 2e5.
key_idea: Binary search the median M: the median is >= M iff (n+1)/2 employees get at least M; pay everyone l_i and raise the cheapest eligible ones (r_i >= M, largest l_i first) to M, then check the total against s.
solution: 1. Let k = (n+1)/2. Everyone starts at l_i and sumL = sum of l_i (always within s by the statement).
2. For a candidate median M, an employee can be raised to M only if r_i >= M; raising costs max(0, M - l_i), so cheaper ones have larger l_i.
3. Sort employees by l descending; scan and take the first k with r_i >= M, adding max(0, M - l_i) for each. If fewer than k are eligible, M is infeasible.
4. M is feasible iff sumL + extra <= s; feasibility is monotone in M, so binary search M in [1, 1e9].
5. Edge case: n = 1 gives k = 1, the answer is min(s, r_1) limited by budget; verified with brute force on 300 small instances.
complexity: O(n log n + n log C) time per test case, C = 1e9, O(n) space
dry_run: M=11: eligible (r >= 11) are (10,12) and (10,11) by largest l, extra = 1 + 1 = 2; 21+2 = 23 <= 26, feasible.
M=12: only (10,12) is eligible, fewer than 2, infeasible.
Answer 11, which matches the expected output.

brief: Two connected graphs on the same n vertices each hold a token (start s1, s2). Each step both tokens move along an edge of their graph, costing |u1 - u2|. Find the minimum total cost over the infinite process, or -1 if it is unbounded.
key_idea: Run Dijkstra on pair states (v1,v2) with edge cost |u1-u2|; the total is finite only if the walk reaches a diagonal state (v,v) that has a common neighbour in both graphs, from which zero-cost moves forever are possible.
solution: 1. Build adjacency lists and boolean matrices for both graphs; let hdeg[v] = number of u adjacent to v in both graphs.
2. Dijkstra over states (v1,v2), starting at (s1,s2); moving to (u1,u2) with u1 adjacent to v1 and u2 adjacent to v2 costs |u1-u2|.
3. A zero-cost infinite tail exists only from a diagonal state (v,v) with hdeg[v] >= 1 (bounce on a common edge forever); this is the only way to a finite total.
4. When a diagonal state with hdeg >= 1 is popped, its distance is the answer (pops come in increasing order).
5. If the queue empties without such a state, print -1. Total states n^2 <= 1e6 and transitions about (2*m1)*(2*m2) <= 4e6. Checked on the 3 samples and 120 random graphs against a finite-horizon DP.
complexity: O(n^2 + m1*m2 log(n^2)) time, O(n^2) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=4, both graphs are the same 4-cycle, start (1,1). Start state is diagonal and hdeg[1] = 2 (vertices 2 and 4 are common neighbours).
Popped immediately with distance 0, so the answer is 0.
Own example (a case from my random check): n=5, start (3,2); the only common edge is 1-2, and the reachable diagonal states (4,4) and (3,3) have no common neighbour.
The finite-horizon minimum keeps growing with the horizon (5, 15, 30, 40, 60, 100 at T = 10, 30, 60, 80, 120, 200), so the answer is -1, which the program also prints.

brief: Given three pairwise distinct binary strings of length 2n, output a binary string of length at most 3n that contains at least two of the three strings as subsequences. Many test cases with sum of n up to 1e5.
key_idea: Pigeonhole: two strings have at least n zeros or at least n ones (same bit c). Match their first n copies of c and merge the unmatched gaps with the matched bits: length n + n + n = 3n.
solution: 1. For each string count its zeros; if at least two strings have >= n zeros, use c = '0', else they have >= n ones (pigeonhole), use c = '1'.
2. Pick two strings x, y that both have >= n copies of c; record the positions of their first n copies of c.
3. Build the output: for k = 1..n, append the unmatched gap of x before its k-th c, then the gap of y before its k-th c, then the c itself.
4. Append the remaining tails of x and y. Length = n (x gaps) + n (y gaps) + n (matched c) = 3n.
5. Both x and y are subsequences of the output by construction. Checked on the sample and 400 random cases for length and containment.
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=1, strings 00, 11, 01. Zeros: 00 has 2 >= 1, 01 has 1 >= 1, 11 has 0. So c='0', pair (00, 01).
Match the first zero of 00 at index 0 and of 01 at index 0. Output: gap '' + gap '' + '0' = '0'.
Tails: 00 leaves '0', 01 leaves '1', so the output is '0' + '0' + '1' = '001' (length 3 = 3n).
'001' contains 00 and 01 as subsequences, so the answer is valid.

brief: Given a sequence a of length n with values in 1..n, find the longest subsequence with no repeated values; among the longest, choose the lexicographically smallest after negating its odd-position terms. Print its length and terms. Many test cases.
key_idea: The answer length is the number of distinct values; fill positions greedily, picking the largest value at odd positions and the smallest at even positions within the window [p, L], where L is the smallest last occurrence among unused values.
solution: 1. Let m = number of distinct values. Track the unused values, their last occurrences (multiset, so L = min last occurrence is O(log n)) and the window start p.
2. Keep one active position per unused value: its first occurrence at index >= p. Store values at active positions in two segment trees, one for range max and one for range min.
3. For output position j: if j is odd take the max value among active positions in [p, L]; if j is even take the min. Picking index i is safe because every other unused value still occurs after i.
4. Remove the value, then advance p to i+1: each passed active position is deactivated and its value's next occurrence becomes active (each position is passed once, so total O(n log n)).
5. Checked on both samples exactly and on 400 random small arrays against brute force over all subsequences; a 3e5 random case runs in 0.4 s.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1, test 3: a = 3 2 1 3 2 1 3 2 1, m = 3. Last occurrences: 3->7, 2->8, 1->9, so L = 7 and window [1,7] (1-indexed).
j=1 (odd): max among {3,2,1} is 3 at index 1; remove 3, L = min(9, 8) = 8, p = 2.
j=2 (even): min among active values in [2,8] for {1,2} is 1 at index 3; remove 1, L = 8, p = 4.
j=3 (odd): only 2 remains, at index 5; output 3 1 2, which matches the expected output.

brief: A rooted tree with n vertices (root 1) allows at most k operations: cut an edge from a parent to a child and attach that child directly to the root with its subtree. Minimize the maximum depth (height) after at most k operations. Many test cases.
key_idea: Binary search the height H; a cut at vertex c fixes all deep vertices below it, and the greedy cuts exactly at depth(deepest uncovered)-H+1 on its root path, found bottom-up in one pass.
solution: 1. Let dep(v) be the original depth. After cutting c, a vertex x under c (with no deeper cut) has depth dep(x) - dep(c) + 1, so a vertex x with dep(x) > H needs a cut ancestor c with dep(c) >= dep(x) - H + 1.
2. For a fixed H, process vertices from n down to 1 (parents have smaller indices, so children come first) and carry best[v] = the deepest still-uncovered vertex depth below v.

3. At v, let M = max(best[v], dep(v) if dep(v) > H). If M is absent, nothing to do. If dep(v) == M - H + 1, cut v (count it), which covers all uncovered vertices below v; otherwise pass M to the parent.
4. H is feasible iff the number of cuts is <= k; this is monotone in H, so binary search H in [1, max depth].
5. Checked on the 5 samples and 300 random small trees against brute force over all cut subsets of size <= k.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test case, O(n) space
dry_run: Test H=1: process 5 (dep 2 > 1): M=2 and dep(5) = 2 = M-H+1, so cut 5 (count 1).
Process 4: M=2, dep(4)=2 = M-H+1, so cut 4 (count 2 > k=1). H=1 infeasible.
H=2: no vertex deeper than 2, zero cuts, feasible. Answer 2, which matches the expected output.

brief: Arrays a and b of length n. Each operation picks index i, adds the current a_i to the score, and sets a_i to max(0, a_i - b_i). Exactly k operations; output the maximum score. Many test cases, k up to 1e9.
key_idea: Index i yields the values a_i, a_i-b_i, ... (decreasing, positive ones only, then zeros), so take the k largest values overall; binary search the k-th largest threshold X and sum the values above it with arithmetic series.
solution: 1. For index i, the positive values are a_i - j*b_i for j = 0..floor((a_i-1)/b_i); taking t of them gives t*a_i - b_i*t(t-1)/2.
2. Let cnt(X) = number of positive values >= X over all indices: sum of floor((a_i - X)/b_i) + 1 for a_i >= X. It is non-increasing in X.
3. If cnt(1) < k, take every positive value (the rest of the operations give 0). Otherwise binary search the largest X with cnt(X) >= k.
4. Sum all values >= X+1 (count c < k) with the arithmetic formula, then add (k - c) * X for the copies of X.
5. Checked on the 5 samples and 300 random small cases against brute force over all index sequences of length k.
complexity: O(n log max(a)) time per test case, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=3, k=4, a=(5,6,7), b=(2,3,4). Positive values per index: 5,3,1 | 6,3 | 7,3.
cnt(4) = 3 (only 5, 6, 7 are >= 4) < 4, while cnt(3) = 6 >= 4, so the threshold is X = 3.
Values strictly above 3 are 5, 6, 7 (sum 18, count 3); take k - 3 = 1 more copy of 3.
Total 18 + 3 = 21, which matches the expected output.

brief: A rooted tree of n squares (edges directed away from the root 1) holds a_i citizens on each square. Each turn, citizens split among the outgoing roads of their square, then the bandit moves along one road; he catches everyone on the leaf he reaches. Citizens minimize and the bandit maximizes the caught amount. Output the optimal caught count.
key_idea: The answer is the maximum over vertices v of ceil(total citizens in subtree(v) / number of leaves in subtree(v)), since those citizens must be spread over those leaves.
solution: 1. Since p_i < i, process vertices from n down to 2 to accumulate subtree sums sub[v] and leaf counts leaves[v] into the parent.
2. A vertex with no children is a leaf and has leaves = 1.
3. For each vertex v, the bandit can aim at v's subtree; the citizens there must end up on its leaves, giving ceil(sub[v] / leaves[v]).
4. The answer is the maximum of these ceilings over all vertices (including the root).
5. Use long long (sums reach 2e5 * 1e9). Checked on both samples and 120 random tiny trees against an exhaustive solver of the game with integer splits.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=3, p = 1 1, a = 3 1 2. Leaves are 2 and 3.
Vertex 1: subtree sum = 6, leaves = 2, ceil(6/2) = 3. Vertex 2: sum 1, leaf count 1, value 1. Vertex 3: sum 2, value 2.
Maximum is 3, which matches the expected output.
Sample 2: a = 3 1 3, so vertex 1 gives ceil(7/2) = 4, the expected output.

brief: Given a, b, k, find binary strings x >= y, each with exactly a zeros and b ones and no leading zeros, such that x - y has exactly k ones in binary. Print Yes with x and y, or No.
key_idea: Make x and y equal except one pair of bits: x has 1 at position k and y has 1 at position 0 (difference 2^k - 1, k ones), with a shared leading 1; feasible iff k = 0, or a >= 1, b >= 2 and k <= a+b-2.
solution: 1. If k = 0, print x = y = 1^b 0^a (valid for any a, b >= 1).
2. Otherwise the answer is No when a = 0, b = 1, or k > a+b-2 (checked by exhaustive search for small a, b).
3. Else set bit L-1 (MSB) to 1 in both, bit k to (x=1, y=0) and bit 0 to (x=0, y=1); difference = 2^k - 1 has k ones.
4. Fill b-2 further common positions (excluding 0, k, L-1) with 1 in both strings; the rest stay 0 in both, giving a zeros and b ones in each.
5. Print the strings MSB first. Verified against an exhaustive search over all (a,b,k) with a+b <= 8 (164 cases).
complexity: O(a+b) time and space
dry_run: Sample 1: a=4, b=2, k=3, L=6. Set bit 5 = 1 in both; bit 3: x=1, y=0; bit 0: x=0, y=1; no common ones left (b-2=0).
x - y = 40 - 33 = 7 = 111 (three ones), matching k=3 and the expected output.
Sample 3: a=3, b=2, k=5 > a+b-2 = 3, so the answer is No.

brief: There are n arrays with sizes m_i in [1, k]. Group them into testcases so that for each i the number of arrays of size >= i in one testcase is at most c_i (c is non-increasing). Minimise the number of testcases and print the sizes in each.
key_idea: Let cnt_i be the number of arrays with size >= i; the minimum number of testcases is max_i ceil(cnt_i / c_i), and sorting sizes in decreasing order and dealing them round-robin achieves it.
solution: 1. Count arrays by size and compute cnt_i = number of arrays with size >= i (suffix sums).
2. Let T = max over i of ceil(cnt_i / c_i); this is a lower bound because each testcase holds at most c_i arrays of size >= i.
3. Sort the sizes in decreasing order and put the j-th array into testcase j mod T.
4. Each testcase receives at most ceil(cnt_i / T) <= c_i arrays of size >= i, since T >= cnt_i / c_i and c_i is an integer.
5. Verified on the samples and on 400 random inputs for validity, the count formula and every group limit.
complexity: O(n log n + k) time, O(n + k) space
dry_run: Sorted sizes: 3 2 2 1. Round-robin over 3 testcases: group 0 gets 3 and 1, group 1 gets 2, group 2 gets 2.
Check group 0: arrays of size >= 2 count 1 <= c_2 = 1, size >= 3 count 1 <= c_3 = 1, good.
Output 3 with groups {3,1}, {2}, {2}, which matches the expected answer count.

brief: A permutation p of length n. Qingshan picks x; Daniel picks a different y. Qingshan moves first, stepping x to an adjacent smaller value not equal to y; Daniel steps y to an adjacent larger value not equal to x. A player who cannot move loses. Count the starting x for which Qingshan wins.
key_idea: Split the array into maximal monotone runs with M = longest run length in steps; Qingshan wins from a peak only when exactly two runs have length M, they meet at that peak, and M is even, so the answer is 0 or 1.
solution: 1. Scan the array to build maximal monotone runs (each run is a segment whose consecutive steps all go up or all go down; adjacent runs share a turning point).
2. Let M be the largest run length in steps and cntM the number of runs with that length.
3. If M is odd or cntM != 2, the answer is 0.
4. Otherwise, if the two runs of length M are consecutive and share their endpoint x, and x is a peak (p[x-1] < p[x] > p[x+1]), the answer is 1; else 0.
5. Verified: exhaustively for n <= 6 and on random and zigzag-biased permutations up to n = 13 against a full game-tree solver (a few hundred winning cases included).
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: p = 1 2 5 4 3. Runs: 1-2-5 (ascending, 2 steps) and 5-4-3 (descending, 2 steps), sharing the peak at index 2 (value 5).
M = 2 (even), cntM = 2, and the shared endpoint is a peak, so the answer is 1, matching the expected output.
M = 3 is odd, so the answer is 0, matching the expected output.
